angel-share.definition: The portion of whiskey that evaporates from the cask during maturation. In cool Scotland it runs roughly 2% per year; in tropical India and Taiwan it can exceed 8–12%.
angel-share.why: Heat speeds the spirit's interaction with the cask, and the heavy evaporation that comes with it concentrates what remains. Together they are why young tropical-climate whiskeys can taste older than their age statements, at the cost of losing volume fast.

peat.definition: Decomposed, waterlogged vegetation (often centuries of moss and heather) cut from bogs, dried and burned to dry malted barley. Smoke compounds deposit on the grain and carry through distillation.
peat.why: Peat's character depends on what decomposed into it: Islay's moss-and-sedge peat gives more of the medicinal phenols (cresols, guaiacol), while woodier, heather-rich mainland peat reads softer and more like a wood fire. Seaweed in the peat is a popular myth.

phenol-ppm.definition: A measure of smoke compounds in the malted barley. Islay's heavily peated malts run roughly 30–55 ppm; unpeated 'malt' is under 1–3 ppm.
phenol-ppm.why: Much of the peat character actually falls away by the time the spirit reaches the cask, so a high ppm barley does not mean a proportionally smokier pour.

mashbill.definition: The grain recipe for American whiskey. Bourbon must be at least 51% corn; rye at least 51% rye. The remainder is typically rye, wheat or barley.
mashbill.why: The flavor grain defines the style: corn gives caramel sweetness, rye gives dry spice, and wheat gives softness. This single choice shapes the entire pour.

charred-barrel.definition: American oak barrels for bourbon are flame-charred inside (level 1 to 4; level 4 is called 'alligator char' for its cracked texture). Charred wood acts as both flavor source and filter.
charred-barrel.why: Charring caramelizes wood sugars into a red layer that dissolves into the spirit, and the carbon char strips harsh sulfur compounds. Legally, bourbon must use new charred oak containers.

lincoln-county.definition: The Tennessee whiskey requirement that new spirit drips through sugar-maple charcoal before barreling.
lincoln-county.why: The law applies to whiskey labeled Tennessee whiskey, with named exemptions (e.g. Prichard's, which uses a different process); and the two big houses differ in technique — Jack Daniel's drips room-temperature spirit through the charcoal, while George Dickel chills the whisky first.

bottled-in-bond.definition: A US legal standard from 1897: the whiskey must be at least 4 years old, exactly 100 proof (50% ABV), the product of one distilling season — January–June or July–December of a single year — from one distiller at one distillery, aged in a US bonded warehouse.
bottled-in-bond.why: Created to guarantee authenticity in an era of doctored whiskey; today it signals honest age and full flavor at a fair price.

nas.definition: A whiskey bottled without declaring a minimum age, usually because it blends older and younger casks or responds to stock pressure.
nas.why: Age statements guarantee a floor, not quality: cask type, warehouse and peating can matter more. NAS bottlings range from cynical to brilliant.

cask-strength.definition: Whiskey bottled at its natural cask strength, undiluted (typically 50–60% ABV) except for evaporation.
cask-strength.why: No water is added before bottling, so you choose the dilution; a few drops in the glass often release aromas the high alcohol holds back.

chill-filtration.definition: Cooling whiskey to near freezing and filtering out fatty acids and esters so it stays clear when ice is added.
chill-filtration.why: It keeps the whiskey clear when cold or diluted. Whether it removes noticeable flavour is debated; many enthusiasts prefer non-chill-filtered bottlings, which can turn hazy with water or ice. Bottlings at 46% and above generally don't need it.

mizunara.definition: Japan's indigenous oak, Quercus mongolica var. grosseserrata (also called Q. crispula or mizunara oak). It was first used out of necessity when imported casks were scarce during the Second World War; it is porous and leak-prone, and difficult to cooper.
mizunara.why: Mizunara's lactones and eugenols read as sandalwood, incense and coconut; it became the signature of premium Japanese whisky — a limit born of difficulty.

pot-still-character.definition: The creamy, lightly spicy texture of Irish whiskey distilled from a mash of both malted and unmalted barley in a pot still.
pot-still-character.why: The unmalted barley tradition began as a tax dodge on malt, and it happened to create a texture no other country replicates.

worm-tub.definition: A traditional condenser: a long copper coil submerged in a cold water tank, still used at a handful of Scottish distilleries.
worm-tub.why: Worm tubs condense vapor quickly with limited copper contact, preserving a meaty, sulfur-adjacent weight that modern condensers remove.

sour-mash.definition: The American practice of adding a portion of the previous fermentation's acidic spent mash to the new one, keeping pH consistent.
sour-mash.why: A stable pH prevents bacterial takeover between batches; nearly all bourbon is sour mash, so the label says less than people assume.

whisky-vs-whiskey.definition: Scotland, Japan and Canada write 'whisky'; Ireland and the USA write 'whiskey'. This app uses 'whiskey' as its own global default and follows each region's convention in its own copy.
whisky-vs-whiskey.why: The spelling is a linguistic inheritance of Scotch vs Irish emigration, not a quality or style difference.

japanese-whisky-standard.definition: The Japan Spirits & Liqueurs Makers Association's voluntary labeling standards (issued February 2021): for a bottle to be labeled 'Japanese whisky', raw materials must be malted, fermented and distilled in Japan, matured there for at least three years, and bottled in Japan. Full member effect came in April 2024.
japanese-whisky-standard.why: This is why some bottles made in Japan — like Nikka From the Barrel, which includes selected imported whisky — are honestly labeled 'Japan-made' rather than 'Japanese whisky': the standard is raw-material based, not just distillery location.

grain-whiskey.definition: Whiskey distilled from a mash of cereal grains — typically maize or wheat with some malted barley — in a continuous column still, producing a lighter, higher-proof spirit than pot-still distillation.
grain-whiskey.why: Grain whiskey is the body of nearly every blended category: it lightens the blend and carries the character of the malt components. Column distillation runs continuously, unlike the batch process of pot stills.
